ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
At each of the vertices of a cube sits a Bunchkin. Two Bunchkins are said to be adjacent if and only if they sit at either end of one of the cube's edges. Each Bunchkin is either a 'truther', who always tells the truth, or a 'liar', who always lies. All eight Bunchkins say 'I am adjacent to exactly two liars'. What is the maximum number of Bunchkins who are telling the truth?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: the attached images show a cube, which corresponds to a graph with 8 vertices and each vertex adjacent to 3 others. Reasoning: Model the cube as a graph where each Bunchkin is a vertex of degree 3. Let T be the number of truthers and L = 8 - T be the number of liars. Every truther's statement is true, so each truther is adjacent to exactly 2 liars. Therefore the number of truther-liar edges is 2T. Now count edge-incidences from the liar side. There are 3L = 3(8 - T) total incidences touching liars. These consist of the 2T incidences from truther-liar edges plus 2e_LL incidences from liar-liar edges, where e_LL is the number of liar-liar edges. Hence 3(8 - T) = 2T + 2e_LL, so 24 - 5T = 2e_LL. Since e_LL >= 0, we get 24 - 5T >= 0, so T <= 4.8. Since T is an integer, T <= 4. To show 4 is attainable, choose the four truthers to be the endpoints of two disjoint parallel cube edges that are not adjacent to each other, for example two opposite parallel edges. Then each truther has exactly one truther-neighbor and two liar-neighbors, so each truther tells the truth. Each liar then has exactly one liar-neighbor, not exactly two, so each liar is lying. Thus 4 truthers can occur and no more than 4 can occur.

Count all edge incidences from the liar side: there are 3L=3(8-T) incidences, consisting of the 2T truther-liar incidences plus twice the number of liar-liar edges. Therefore the maximum is 4.

method.method_draft: Use the bipartite structure of the cube: color the cube vertices black and white so every edge connects opposite colors, with 4 vertices of each color. A truther has degree 3 and says the truth, so it must have exactly 2 liar-neighbors and therefore exactly 1 truther-neighbor. Hence the subgraph formed by the truthers must be a matching, so the number of truthers is even and the truthers are equally split between the two color classes. Check possible values above 4: 8 truthers is impossible because then no one has liar-neighbors. If there were 6 truthers, then each color class would contain 3 truthers and only 1 liar. But any truther’s neighbors all lie in the opposite color class, and there would be only one opposite-colored liar available, not the required two. Thus more than 4 truthers is impossible. Finally, exhibit 4 truthers on two disjoint cube edges chosen so that each truther has one truther-neighbor and two liar-neighbors; the remaining liars each have not exactly two liar-neighbors. So the maximum is 4.
method.CoT_raw:
The image shows the graph of a cube: 8 vertices, each vertex connected by edges to 3 adjacent vertices. Use the cube's bipartite structure: color vertices black and white so every edge joins opposite colors, with 4 vertices of each color.

A truther says, truthfully, "I am adjacent to exactly two liars." Since every cube vertex has degree 3, each truther must have exactly 2 liar-neighbors and therefore exactly 1 truther-neighbor. Thus, in the subgraph induced by the truthers, every truther has degree exactly 1. So the truthers form a matching: they are paired along disjoint cube edges. Therefore the number of truthers is even, and since every matching edge in a bipartite graph uses one black and one white vertex, the truthers are equally split between the two color classes.

Now rule out more than 4 truthers. If all 8 were truthers, then no one would have any liar-neighbors, so their statement would be false. If there were 6 truthers, then by the matching/equal-split condition, there would be 3 truthers in each color class and only 1 liar in each color class. But every truther's three neighbors lie in the opposite color class, where there is only 1 liar total, so no truther could be adjacent to exactly 2 liars. Thus 6 truthers is impossible. Hence at most 4 truthers are possible.

Finally, 4 truthers can be achieved. For example, choose two opposite parallel edges of the cube, and put truthers on their four endpoints. Each truther is adjacent to its paired truther on the same chosen edge and to two liars, so each truther tells the truth. The remaining four vertices are liars; in this arrangement each liar has only 1 liar-neighbor, not exactly 2, so each liar's statement is false. Therefore the maximum number of truthers is 4.
